vignette:
He first came to the war zone as a Navy officer with the confidence of someone who has spent most of his adult life in structured places, where rank, routine, and procedure can hold chaos at bay. At 55, he still carries himself with the discipline of military life, speaking carefully and watching his surroundings as if he is always taking in more than he says. He is Latin American, in a long-term relationship now, and has built a life that looks steady from the outside. But as he tells the story, the steadiness is something he works hard to maintain, especially since the years he spent moving through a civilian area of war.

He had gone there expecting hardship, but not the particular kind of helplessness that came from being a noncombatant in a city where ordinary life had been torn apart. He remembers the first days in vivid fragments: the smell of smoke clinging to clothes, the constant strain of listening for distant explosions, the sight of families carrying bags and children through streets that had become checkpoints. He was trained to assess risk, yet the danger there felt shapeless. It could be in the next building, the next car, the next person running toward him with an urgent warning. He recalls trying to stay useful, trying to remain calm for the civilians around him, while privately feeling that the ground itself had become unstable.

The event that still organizes his memory happened during a period of intense movement through the city. He describes being caught near an area where fighting broke out suddenly, with no clear warning and no safe route visible. Civilians scattered in every direction. A woman fell near him, and he remembers turning toward her just as the sound of gunfire and screaming overwhelmed everything else. He does not always narrate the scene in order; instead, he comes back to certain details with a kind of stunned precision: the look on people's faces, the way his body moved before his mind could catch up, the feeling that he was responsible for helping while also knowing he could not protect everyone. What haunts him most is not one single image, but the accumulation of moments in which he felt frozen between action and helplessness.

Afterward, he returns to duty in appearance, but something in him has narrowed. He starts sleeping lightly, waking at the smallest sound. He checks doors and windows repeatedly, even in places he knows are safe. In his current life, the habits show up in ordinary settings: he notices exits immediately in restaurants, scans parking lots before getting out of the car, and becomes tense when loud motorcycles backfire or a television sound effect suddenly erupts. He says his body reacts before he can explain why, with his chest tightening and his muscles bracing as if he is still abroad and still listening for the next blast.

At home, his partner notices that he is often elsewhere, even when sitting right in front of her. He loves her and wants closeness, but he also feels himself pulling back when conversations touch on the war zone or on anything that makes him remember how little control he had. He becomes irritable over small things, then ashamed of the sharpness in his tone. At times, he feels guilty for surviving when civilians did not, especially when he thinks of the people he could not save. He avoids news footage from conflict zones, yet he cannot seem to stop himself from looking when images appear on a screen. The sight makes his stomach drop, and afterward he is left with a heaviness that can last for hours.

He does not talk easily about fear. In the Navy, he learned to function through it. But in private, he admits that he is tired in a way that rest does not fix. The war zone is no longer his present environment, yet it continues to intrude in flashes, dreams, and sudden sensations that leave him disoriented. He can be standing in a grocery store and, for a moment, feel the same urgency he felt when civilians ran through the street. He knows he is safe now, and still his body often does not believe it.
